diagnostic_evidence.quote: where $\Gamma(h, f) = h \gL(h^{-1} f) - f \gL h^{-1}$ is the carr\'e du champ operator associated with the generator $\gL$

issues.failure_explanation: For arbitrary lambda, L^{h,lambda}f = h^{-1}L(hf) - lambda f is generally not conservative (L^{h,lambda}1 = h^{-1}Lh - lambda is not 0), so it does not generate a Markov process with a probability path measure. The Radon-Nikodym formula (eq:doob) contains no lambda, so it cannot hold for every lambda. In the 'in particular' part, the displayed Gamma(h,f) = hL(h^{-1}f) - fLh^{-1} is not the carré du champ. Gamma(h,f) = L(hf) - hLf - fLh is needed for L^{h,lambda}f = Lf + h^{-1}Gamma(h,f).
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restrict the theorem to lambda = h^{-1}Lh (or add the exponential lambda-term to the density and a conservativeness requirement), and replace Gamma by L(hf) - hLf - fLh.
issues.overall_effect: The cited tool is misstated. The paper only uses the conservative case lambda = h^{-1}Lh, so its own results are not affected.
issues.title: Doob h-transform stated for arbitrary lambda; Radon-Nikodym derivative ignores lambda; wrong carré du champ formula
issues.why_classification: Local restatement; all downstream uses are already in the conservative case.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: we set the drift $\vb_t(\vx) \equiv \vzero$ and the diffusion coefficient $\mD_t(\vx) \equiv \vzero$

issues.failure_explanation: Courrège's theorem only yields a positive semidefinite diffusion matrix, not a positive definite one. The theorem, and Assumptions ass:regularity_diffusion and ass:regularity_levy, demand positive definiteness. The Lévy-Itô example and the jump experiment take D ≡ 0, and finite-state jump chains also have D = 0. So the stated hypotheses contradict the claimed scope of 'arbitrary Lévy-type processes'.

failure_location.quote: $\mD_t(\vx)$ is the diffusion coefficient which positive definite for any $\vx \in \R^d$

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace 'positive definite' by 'positive semidefinite' in the theorem and assumptions, and check which later steps (e.g. diffusion-part computations) need uniform ellipticity.
issues.overall_effect: The characterization and its regularity assumptions as stated do not cover the jump and Lévy-Itô instances, nor the GBM example.
issues.title: Levy-type generator theorem requires positive definite D, excluding pure-jump models used in the paper
issues.why_classification: A local weakening of the hypothesis; the method and conclusions are unchanged.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: The diffusion matrix $\mD_t(\vx)$ is positive definite and satisfies that $D_t^{ij} \in C^{2,0}(\R^d)$ for any $i, j \in [d]$ and $\vx \in \R^d$

issues.failure_explanation: For GBM, D(x) = diag(x) Σ Σ^T diag(x) is quadratic in x. It is unbounded, so it is not in the bounded-derivative class C^{2,0}. It is degenerate (not positive definite) on the boundary of the positive orthant. The state space R^d_+ is not R^d, and the function classes U and V of the appendix were built for R^d. So the stated assumptions are not verified, and fail as written.

failure_location.quote: Thus, this choice clearly fits within our denoising Markov model framework, with a diffusion process as the forward dynamics.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Either verify a modified set of assumptions on R^d_+ (weighted function spaces, boundary behaviour) or state that the GBM example is heuristic.
issues.overall_effect: The theory (time reversal, change of measure, KL bound) is not shown to apply to the GBM experiment. The experiment is only heuristically linked to the guarantees.
issues.title: GBM forward process claimed to fit the framework though regularity assumptions fail
issues.why_classification: Requires a contained extension of the verification of assumptions for one example, or a scope weakening.

issues.failure_explanation: The ratio identity ŝ(y_k,y) = ŝ(ref,y)/ŝ(ref,y_k) is correct. However, the integrand also contains λ(‖y − y_k‖), which is centered at y_k. Hence J(y_k) = ∫ŝ(ref,y)λ(‖y − y_k‖)dy / ŝ(ref,y_k), which differs from J(ref)/ŝ(ref,y_k), where λ is centered at y_ref. The claimed formula is false for general kernels, so the jump rates and the Poisson counts of the backward simulation are miscomputed.

failure_location.quote: one can reuse numerical integrations as

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Compute J(y) as a convolution of ŝ(ref,·) with the kernel (e.g. one FFT per time step, as in the torus case) and divide by ŝ(ref,y_k), instead of reusing J at y_ref.
issues.overall_effect: The proposed efficient backward simulation of the jump model is incorrect as described and gives wrong total jump rates.
issues.title: Reuse of the jump-rate integral across samples is invalid because the kernel is centered at the sample
issues.why_classification: A contained computational correction (convolution/FFT) exists, but the stated shortcut is lost.

issues.failure_explanation: The Palmowski–Rolski density contains the boundary factor η_0(x_T)/η_T(x_0). The proof deletes it by Dynkin's formula, which is an identity for expectations. Pathwise, log η_{T-t}(x_t) − log η_T(x_0) = ∫L̃ log η ds plus a nonzero martingale term. So the stated density (eq:radon_nikodym), with no boundary term, is not the Radon-Nikodym derivative of Q with respect to P, nor is dP/dQ. Only the expected log-density, i.e. the KL value, might survive after taking expectations. Conditional or sub-interval uses (as in the proof of thm:numerical_error) need the pathwise density.

failure_location.quote: where the last equality is by Dynkin's formula (\cref{thm:dynkin}).

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Keep the boundary factor in the density and the martingale term. Prove E[log dP/dQ] = L[η] by taking expectations, and justify the interval-wise conditional bounds with the correct density.
issues.overall_effect: The stated Radon-Nikodym derivative and its dependent conditional KL bounds are not justified pathwise. The KL identity requires a separate expectation-level argument with the boundary and martingale terms.
issues.title: Pathwise Radon-Nikodym derivative obtained from Dynkin's formula, which holds only in expectation
issues.why_classification: A contained corrective argument keeps the results essentially intact, but it requires a new lemma-level argument.
